Mammoth Lakes, California Vacation Guide: Best Rentals & Hotels - 2026

Mammoth Lakes at a Glance

Mammoth Lakes is a year-round mountain town in California's Eastern Sierra, and its calendar basically splits in two: winter skiing on one side, summer alpine adventure on the other. The right home base depends on which season brought you there. For winter ski trips, book Village-area lodging. For summer hiking and fishing trips, look at Old Mammoth or one of the cabins in the lakes basin instead. Proximity to the right trailhead or lift matters more here than almost anywhere else in California.

Sitting at roughly 7,880 feet elevation along US-395, Mammoth Lakes built its reputation on Mammoth Mountain, one of the tallest and latest-closing ski resorts in North America. But the town has grown into a legitimate four-season destination in its own right. Summer brings wildflower meadows, granite lake basins, and access to Devils Postpile National Monument. Winter turns that same terrain into deep-powder ski runs served by an extensive lift network. Because the town is compact, most vacation rentals and hotels sit within a 10-minute drive of both the ski area and the summer trailheads. That's a big part of why Mammoth works so well as a single-base trip rather than something you'd break into multiple stops.

Getting to Mammoth Lakes: Flying vs. the Drive from LA

Most visitors reach Mammoth Lakes by driving up US-395 from Southern California. The trip from Los Angeles covers roughly 300 miles and takes about five hours under normal conditions, longer if you stop in Bishop or Lone Pine along the way. The drive is scenic, but it's exposed to winter storms, so check Caltrans chain-control reports before a winter departure and carry chains even if your vehicle has all-wheel drive. Closures on Sherwin Grade and Deadman Summit are common during heavy snow.

Flying is the faster option when it's available. Mammoth Yosemite Airport (MMH) receives seasonal nonstop service from Los Angeles and other hubs during the winter months, cutting travel time to under 90 minutes in the air. Schedules shift year to year, though, and flights can be limited or canceled outside peak ski season. If you're flying in without a rental car reserved, or if your group is large enough to want door-to-door service instead of driving a rental up the mountain in snow, arranging private airport transportation in advance is worth doing. Travelers connecting through Los Angeles hubs before heading to the Sierra should book the LAX-to-Mammoth or LAX-to-Bishop leg well ahead, as same-day availability on that route is thin.

Village at Mammoth vs. Old Mammoth: Where to Stay

Lodging in Mammoth Lakes splits into two distinct neighborhoods, and picking the right one shapes the whole trip. The Village at Mammoth is the walkable, condo-dense core built around the gondola that connects directly to Mammoth Mountain's ski runs. Stay here and you can walk to the lift in ski boots, with restaurants, bars, and the summer farmers market just steps away. That convenience comes at a premium, though, and you'll deal with more foot traffic during peak weeks.

Old Mammoth Road, by contrast, is a quieter residential corridor a short drive from both the Village and Canyon Lodge. It's popular with families and repeat visitors who want a cabin-style vacation rental with a yard or a hot tub rather than a condo tower. It's also closer to the Sherwin Creek area trailheads, which makes it a strong choice for summer hiking and mountain biking trips. Most vacation rental searches on Vrbo let you filter by neighborhood, so decide on Village versus Old Mammoth before you start browsing listings rather than after. It narrows the search considerably and helps you compare true walk-to-lift or walk-to-trail properties against each other.

Winter in Mammoth Lakes: Skiing and Mammoth Mountain's Long Season

Mammoth Mountain is the reason most winter visitors come to town, and it earns its reputation. With a base elevation near 7,953 feet and a summit above 11,000 feet, the terrain holds snow later into the year than almost any other resort in the state. It's common for Mammoth to stay open into June, and in exceptionally heavy snow years the resort has pushed operations into July. That makes it one of the few places in California where you can reasonably plan a late-spring ski trip. The mountain is also part of the Ikon Pass network, so pass holders from other Ikon resorts can ski Mammoth without buying a separate lift ticket. Worth factoring into your budget if you already hold a pass from a home mountain elsewhere.

Because the season runs so long, book lodging and rental cars well ahead of major holiday weeks, particularly Presidents' Day week and any period with a fresh storm forecast. Both hotel rooms and vacation rentals near the Village sell out fast when powder is in the forecast. If Mammoth's dates or availability don't line up with your trip, Lake Tahoe is the other major California ski option worth comparing. Our Lake Tahoe vacation guide breaks down the North Shore versus South Shore resorts for travelers weighing the two regions against each other.

Summer in Mammoth Lakes: Devils Postpile, Rainbow Falls, and the June Lake Loop

Summer in Mammoth Lakes trades ski runs for alpine lakes and volcanic geology. The most distinctive stop in the area is Devils Postpile National Monument, a wall of blue-gray basalt columns formed by cooling lava roughly 100,000 years ago. From mid-June through early September, access to the monument runs through a mandatory shuttle from the Mammoth Mountain Adventure Center, since the access road is too narrow for the volume of summer traffic. The shuttle also stops near the trailhead for Rainbow Falls, a 101-foot waterfall on the Middle Fork San Joaquin River about two miles further down the trail.

Beyond the monument, the Mammoth Lakes Basin itself, including Twin Lakes, Lake Mary, and Horseshoe Lake, offers easy lakeside walks, canoe rentals, and trout fishing within a few minutes of town. About 20 minutes north, the June Lake Loop is a 16-mile scenic byway off Highway 158 that circles June Lake, Gull Lake, Silver Lake, and Grant Lake. It's a favorite for a slower-paced afternoon drive with fewer crowds than the main Mammoth basin. Roughly 25 minutes further north near Lee Vining, Mono Lake's South Tufa Reserve shows off the lake's namesake calcium-carbonate tufa towers, an ancient saline lake ecosystem that looks nothing like anywhere else in California and makes a natural add-on to a June Lake Loop day trip.

Vacation Rentals in Mammoth Lakes

Vacation rentals are the dominant lodging choice in Mammoth Lakes for families and ski groups, largely because condos and cabins here routinely include ski lockers, hot tubs, and full kitchens. Those amenities matter after a long day on the mountain or the trail. Village-area condos tend to run smaller but put you within walking distance of the gondola, while Old Mammoth and Snowcreek-area rentals offer more square footage and privacy at a lower nightly rate, trading a short drive for extra space.

Book winter-week rentals at least two to three months ahead, since inventory near the Village tightens dramatically once storm cycles start showing up in the forecast. Summer weekends around the Fourth of July and Labor Day fill up nearly as fast with hiking and mountain-biking groups. If you're comparing options, browse Mammoth Lakes vacation rentals on Vrbo to filter by neighborhood, hot tub availability, and walk-to-lift distance, or find your perfect vacation rental on Vrbo if you want to compare pet-friendly cabins near the lakes basin against Village condos side by side.

Best Hotels in Mammoth Lakes

For travelers who prefer daily housekeeping and a front desk over a self-catered condo, Mammoth Lakes has a solid range of hotels clustered mainly in and around the Village and along Old Mammoth Road and Main Street. Village-adjacent hotels put you closest to the gondola and restaurant row, while properties along Main Street and Old Mammoth Road tend to offer better winter rates and easier parking for larger vehicles. That matters if you're arriving with roof-mounted ski boxes or towing a trailer of gear.

Room rates swing hard between low season and peak ski weeks, sometimes doubling between a quiet October weekday and a February powder weekend, so flexibility on travel dates can meaningfully cut your lodging cost. When you're ready to compare rates, you can save 10% or more on hotels with Member Prices through Hotels.com's loyalty pricing, or compare hotel deals on Hotels.com to check current availability against the exact dates of your trip before booking a vacation rental instead.

Planning Your Trip: Getting Around Once You're There

Mammoth Lakes runs a free public trolley system during peak winter and summer seasons that connects the Village, Canyon Lodge, and several lodging areas along Old Mammoth Road. It can genuinely cut down on the need for a rental car if you're staying centrally and mainly want to ski or hit the main trailheads. That said, if your itinerary includes day trips out to June Lake, Devils Postpile's shuttle departure point, or Mono Lake, having your own vehicle or arranging a private car and driver for the day is far more practical than relying on transit.

For groups flying into a Southern California hub and driving up, or for anyone who wants a chauffeured vehicle waiting at Mammoth Yosemite Airport instead of picking up a rental counter car, arrange transportation before you land. Larger groups traveling together often do better in a Mercedes Sprinter van or a Chevrolet Suburban than in multiple separate cars, especially when hauling ski bags and boot bags for a full family. Shuttle and private car options vary by season for travelers connecting through MMH, and Reno-Tahoe International Airport is a practical alternate gateway when MMH weather closes the field.

Frequently Asked Questions

How far is Mammoth Lakes from Los Angeles?

Mammoth Lakes is about 300 miles from Los Angeles via US-395, and the drive typically takes around five hours without stops or winter delays.

Is it better to fly or drive to Mammoth Lakes?

Driving from Southern California takes about five hours but gives you flexibility, while flying into Mammoth Yosemite Airport (MMH) is faster when seasonal nonstop flights are running, typically during winter ski season.

Should I stay in the Village at Mammoth or Old Mammoth?

Stay in the Village at Mammoth if you want to walk to the gondola and restaurants; choose Old Mammoth Road if you prefer more space, quieter surroundings, and easier access to summer trailheads at a lower nightly rate.

When does Mammoth Mountain's ski season end?

Mammoth Mountain often stays open into June and, in heavy snow years, has extended operations into July, making it one of California's longest ski seasons.

How do I visit Devils Postpile National Monument?

From mid-June through early September, visitors must take the mandatory shuttle from the Mammoth Mountain Adventure Center, since private vehicle access on the narrow road is restricted during peak summer traffic.

What is the June Lake Loop?

The June Lake Loop is a 16-mile scenic drive off Highway 158, about 20 minutes north of Mammoth Lakes, circling June Lake, Gull Lake, Silver Lake, and Grant Lake.

How far is Mono Lake from Mammoth Lakes?

Mono Lake's South Tufa Reserve near Lee Vining is roughly 25 to 30 minutes north of Mammoth Lakes, making it an easy add-on to a June Lake Loop day trip.

Are vacation rentals or hotels better for a Mammoth Lakes ski trip?

Vacation rentals generally suit families and groups better because they include kitchens, ski lockers, and often hot tubs, while hotels offer daily housekeeping and are convenient for shorter trips or solo travelers.

Is there public transportation within Mammoth Lakes?

Yes, Mammoth Lakes operates a free trolley system during peak winter and summer seasons connecting the Village, Canyon Lodge, and Old Mammoth Road lodging areas.

What is the elevation of Mammoth Lakes?

The town of Mammoth Lakes sits at roughly 7,880 feet elevation, with Mammoth Mountain's base near 7,953 feet and its summit above 11,000 feet.

Is Lake Tahoe a good alternative to Mammoth Lakes for skiing?

Yes, Lake Tahoe is California's other major ski destination and offers both North Shore and South Shore resort options, making it worth comparing against Mammoth if your travel dates or lodging needs differ.
